newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Missing sheep ship has probably sunk - AMLC [CORRECTED 18:31 GMT].
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Missing sheep ship has probably sunk - AMLC [CORRECTED 18:31 GMT].

text.p: A burning ship carrying almost 70,000 live Australian sheep missing in the Indian Ocean has probably sunk, an Australian livestock official said on Monday.
However, a scaled down search for the ship, missing since last Monday when its crew abandoned it, would continue.

One of the two rescue ships had abandoned the search, but a more sophisticated salvage tug was expected to continue, Lloyd Beeby, a spokesman for the Australian Meat and Livestock Corp (AMLC), told Reuters.

"Yes," Beeby said when asked if it was likely that the ship had sunk. "My understanding is that the tug has very sophisticated equipment and it would certainly have most likely been found by now," he said.
A spokesman for Australian Primary Industries Minister John Anderson said that while the incident was regrettable, the live animal export trade was too valuable to abandon.
"The short answer is that there will not be a ban to this trade. No way," he said. Australia exports a total of 5.54 million live sheep each year, mostly bound for the Middle East.
The 14,990 tonne Panama-flagged Swiss-owned Uniceb was carrying 67,000 head of sheep bound for Australia's biggest live sheep market, Jordan, when fire broke out in its engine room on Monday.
One crewman was killed and the others abandoned the ship some 400 km (245 miles) east of the Seychelles off the east African coast.
(Corrects to make clear Seychelles is off the east coast of Africa, not the north coast).
Despite three days of searching, there has been no trace of the Uniceb.
The incident has sparked calls by animal liberation groups to abandon the live animal export trade.
"This is a regrettable accident, however, our live meat exports are extremely valuable to the nation's economy, particularly rural Australia," a spokesman for Anderson said.
"All up it's worth about half a billion dollars a year, including live cattle and live sheep. The sheep last year were worth A$207 million", he said.
But Jo Bell, director of Animal Liberation, said her organisation was optimistic that the live animal trade would be banned and was increasing pressure on government.
"Our telephone has been running hot in the past few days. It's something that's roused people, there's a big public response on this one," Bell said.
"With this kind of pressure, and particularly because they can't even find the ship, there's a fair chance this (the trade) will end," she said.
Eventually the government would stop the trade because "some things become just too unpopular to be viable", she said.
The animals could very well be slaughtered in Australia according to religious principals of the Middle East buyers, Bell said.
But Bell's views are not shared in the meat trade. AMLC's Beeby said it would be very unlikely that the Uniceb incident would have a long-term effect on the live animal trade.
"From the corporation's point of view, we would be very unlikely to propose any restriction because of it. We see it very clearly as a one-off disaster," Beeby said.
The Maritime Union of Australia, while more concerned with conditions for crews than for live cargo, is supporting Australia's animal rights groups.
But Trevor Charles, Australia co-ordinator for the International Transport Workers' Federation, said "we might be pushing against the wind" to have the government ban the trade.

The Uniceb disaster is Australia's worst live sheep trade death. In 1980 the Farid Fares carrying nearly 41,000 sheep caught fire and sank off the southern coast of Australia en route from Tasmania to Iran. The entire cargo perished.
-- Sydney newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
